p.src:
Begin with one spin in a magnetic field along the $z$-axis. In units with $\hbar=1$, $H=\frac{\omega}{2}\sigma_z,
\qquad
E_+=+\frac{\omega}{2},
\qquad
E_-=-\frac{\omega}{2}.$ The two levels are separated by $\Delta E=E_+-E_-=\omega.$ When the radiation field is included, a spin in the upper level may fall to the lower level and emit a photon of energy $\omega$. A spin already in the lower level has no lower spin state into which it can radiate.

p.src: The subtle case is a spin prepared sideways. A classical magnetic rotor has a continuously varying energy proportional to the cosine of its angle with the field. It precesses at angular frequency $\omega$, radiates at that same frequency, and gradually falls toward its minimum-energy orientation. The total radiated energy depends continuously on the initial angle: an initially horizontal rotor releases half as much energy as one that starts at the top.

p.src:
Quantum mechanics preserves that classical answer only as an average. Write $\ket{\psi}=\alpha\ket{u}+\beta\ket{d},
\qquad
|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1,$ where $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{d}$ are the upper and lower energy eigenstates. The upper component can decay; the lower component cannot. Thus $P(\text{one photon})=|\alpha|^2,
\qquad
P(\text{no photon})=|\beta|^2.$ If a photon is emitted, its energy is the full level spacing $\omega$, not a fraction of it. The mean emitted energy is nevertheless $\expect{E_{\rm emitted}}=|\alpha|^2\omega.$ For a spin along $x$, $|\alpha|^2=|\beta|^2=1/2$, so the mean is $\omega/2$. Each individual event still produces either one photon of energy $\omega$ or no photon. The continuous classical result belongs to the ensemble average; discreteness belongs to each event.

p.src:
Between interventions an isolated state evolves by the Schrödinger equation. Measurement is ordinarily stated as an additional rule. Let $L$ have orthonormal eigenvectors $\ket{\lambda_i}$, and expand $\ket{\psi}=\sum_i\alpha_i\ket{\lambda_i},
\qquad
L\ket{\lambda_i}=\lambda_i\ket{\lambda_i}.$ A measurement yields one value $\lambda_k$ with probability $|\alpha_k|^2$, after which the state is $\ket{\psi}\longrightarrow\ket{\lambda_k}.$ The disappearance of the other components from the post-measurement description is called collapse.

p.src:
The restriction can be seen directly in the coefficients: $c_{uu}c_{dd}=c_{ud}c_{du}
\qquad\text{for every product state}.$ Equivalently, the $2\times2$ coefficient matrix has rank one. Parameter counting reaches the same conclusion. Four complex coefficients contain eight real parameters; normalization removes one and the irrelevant overall phase removes another, leaving six for a general pure two-spin state. Each pure one-spin state needs two real parameters, so two separately specified spins need only four. Product states therefore occupy a special four-parameter subset of the six-parameter two-spin state space. The remaining states are entangled.

p.src:
The familiar one-spin observables must survive inside the larger system. More explicitly, $\sigma_m\equiv\sigma_m\otimes I,
\qquad
\tau_n\equiv I\otimes\sigma_n,
\qquad
m,n\in\{x,y,z\}.$ The abbreviated notation is harmless once the slot convention is fixed. Using $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\\[0.4em]
\sigma_y&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\\[0.4em]
\sigma_z&=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}$ the first-spin operators act while the second label is a spectator: $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x\ket{u\,i}&=\ket{d\,i},
&
\sigma_x\ket{d\,i}&=\ket{u\,i},\\
\sigma_z\ket{u\,i}&=\ket{u\,i},
&
\sigma_z\ket{d\,i}&=-\ket{d\,i}.\end{aligned}$ For the second spin the first label is the spectator: $\begin{aligned}
\tau_x\ket{a\,u}&=\ket{a\,d},
&
\tau_x\ket{a\,d}&=\ket{a\,u},\\
\tau_z\ket{a\,u}&=\ket{a\,u},
&
\tau_z\ket{a\,d}&=-\ket{a\,d}.
\end{aligned}$ The $y$-component also flips its active slot, with $\sigma_y\ket{u}=i\ket{d}$ and $\sigma_y\ket{d}=-i\ket{u}$.

p.src:
For a pure state of one spin, there is always a unit vector $\bm n$ for which $(\bm\sigma\cdot\bm n)\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}.$ Equivalently, the Bloch vector $\bm r
=\bigl(\expect{\sigma_x},\expect{\sigma_y},\expect{\sigma_z}\bigr)$ has length one for a pure one-spin state. Its three components therefore cannot all vanish. Given the state, orienting the detector along $\bm r$ yields $+1$ with certainty. The familiar examples are $z$ for $\ket{u}$, $x$ for $(\ket{u}+\ket{d})/\sqrt2$, and one of the $y$-directions for $(\ket{u}+i\ket{d})/\sqrt2$.

p.src:
Now calculate a local average in the singlet: $\begin{aligned}
\expect{\sigma_z}_S
&=\frac12
(\bra{ud}-\bra{du})\sigma_z
(\ket{ud}-\ket{du})\\
&=\frac12
(\bra{ud}-\bra{du})
(\ket{ud}+\ket{du})\\
&=0.\end{aligned}$ For $\sigma_x$, $\sigma_x\ket{S}
=\frac{\ket{dd}-\ket{uu}}{\sqrt2},$ which is orthogonal to $\ket{S}$, so $\expect{\sigma_x}_S=0$. The phases supplied by $\sigma_y$ do not change that orthogonality, hence $\expect{\sigma_x}_S
=\expect{\sigma_y}_S
=\expect{\sigma_z}_S=0.$ By symmetry, $\expect{\tau_x}_S
=\expect{\tau_y}_S
=\expect{\tau_z}_S=0.$

p.src:
Local averages vanish, so the information in the singlet must reside in joint observables. Start with $\sigma_z\tau_z\ket{ud}=-\ket{ud},
\qquad
\sigma_z\tau_z\ket{du}=-\ket{du}.$ Therefore $\sigma_z\tau_z\ket{S}=-\ket{S},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_z\tau_z}_S=-1.$ The result is not merely an average: the singlet is an eigenstate of the product, so equal-axis $z$-measurements always have opposite signs.

p.src:
Both $x$-operators flip their slots: $\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{ud}=\ket{du},
\qquad
\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{du}=\ket{ud}.$ The exchange of the two terms reverses the antisymmetric state: $\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{S}=-\ket{S},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_x}_S=-1.$ The two phases from the $y$-operators cancel in the same way, giving $\expect{\sigma_y\tau_y}_S=-1.$ By contrast, unequal Cartesian components have zero expectation. For example, $\sigma_x\tau_z\ket{S}
=-\frac{\ket{dd}+\ket{uu}}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_z}_S=0.$ All these results are summarized by $\expect{\sigma_m\tau_n}_S=-\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\expect{(\bm\sigma\cdot\bm a)(\bm\tau\cdot\bm b)}_S
=-\bm a\cdot\bm b.$

\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{du}=\ket{ud}.$ The exchange of the two terms reverses the antisymmetric state: $\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{S}=-\ket{S},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_x}_S=-1.$ The two phases from the $y$-operators cancel in the same way, giving $\expect{\sigma_y\tau_y}_S=-1.$ By contrast, unequal Cartesian components have zero expectation. For example, $\sigma_x\tau_z\ket{S}
=-\frac{\ket{dd}+\ket{uu}}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_z}_S=0.$ All these results are summarized by $\expect{\sigma_m\tau_n}_S=-\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\expect{(\bm\sigma\cdot\bm a)(\bm\tau\cdot\bm b)}_S
=-\bm a\cdot\bm b.$

Both $x$-operators flip their slots: $\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{ud}=\ket{du},
\qquad
\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{du}=\ket{ud}.$ The exchange of the two terms reverses the antisymmetric state: $\sigma_x\tau_x\ket{S}=-\ket{S},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_x}_S=-1.$ The two phases from the $y$-operators cancel in the same way, giving $\expect{\sigma_y\tau_y}_S=-1.$ By contrast, unequal Cartesian components have zero expectation. For example, $\sigma_x\tau_z\ket{S}
=-\frac{\ket{dd}+\ket{uu}}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
\expect{\sigma_x\tau_z}_S=0.$ All these results are summarized by $\expect{\sigma_m\tau_n}_S=-\delta_{mn},
\qquad
\expect{(\bm\sigma\cdot\bm a)(\bm\tau\cdot\bm b)}_S
=-\bm a\cdot\bm b.$

For a product state, joint averages factorize: $\expect{\sigma_m\tau_n}_{\rm prod}
=\expect{\sigma_m}_{\sigma}\expect{\tau_n}_{\tau}.$ The singlet violates this factorization maximally. Each factor on the right would be zero, while an equal-axis product on the left is $-1$. Individually the spins are completely random; jointly, equal components are certainly opposite.

u.src: From Correlation to Bell’s Question
en: From Correlation to Bell’s Question

p.src: Perfect anticorrelation alone is not paradoxical. Imagine placing a penny and a dime in a pocket, distributing one unseen coin to Alice and the other to Bob, and sending them far apart. When Alice sees which coin she has, she immediately knows Bob’s coin. The correlation was established when the coins were together; learning one result sends no signal to the other location.

p.src: The singlet shares that elementary feature but adds a crucial freedom: Alice and Bob may choose any measurement directions, and quantum mechanics predicts the continuously varying correlation $-\bm a\cdot\bm b$. Bell’s theorem asks whether all those correlations can arise from local classical instructions carried by the particles in advance.

p.src: A useful way to sharpen the issue is through simulation. One classical computer can imitate every experiment on one spin: store its state, evolve it with the Schrödinger equation, calculate the requested probabilities, and use a random-number generator to select an outcome. Repeated measurements and magnetic precession can all be reproduced.

p.src: Now split an entangled pair between two classical computers. Allow the computers to interact while the pair is prepared, then disconnect them and choose measurement directions independently at distant locations. No pair of separated local classical programs, even with shared randomness fixed in advance, can reproduce the quantum correlations for every choice of directions. A global classical simulation is possible, but it must keep access to the joint state or otherwise coordinate the two sides in a way that is not a local hidden-variable model.

p.src: This failure of local classical bookkeeping does not provide a faster-than-light communication channel. Alice’s local outcomes remain random, so she cannot control a message that Bob could read without later comparing their records. The terminology surrounding nonlocality varies, but the operational distinction is firm: Bell correlations rule out local classical explanations while preserving no-signaling.

p.src: The composite-state construction has therefore produced something genuinely new. Tensor products preserve the old one-spin physics locally, yet their generic vectors cannot be divided into separate states. In the singlet, all local polarization vanishes while joint spin components carry perfect, basis-independent anticorrelation. The next step is to turn this structure into Bell’s quantitative test of classical reasoning.
